cases.name: 01-windows-bash-grant-wasted-judges
cases.promptMarkdown:
I'm testing my plugin `tidy-notes` on my Windows 11 laptop (Claude Code 2.1.312, native Windows, no WSL installed, Max subscription). The skill normalises a notes file by running a small Python script through Bash and then writing the cleaned file back. From the plugin root I ran:

```
claude plugin eval . --runs 3 --judge-model sonnet --allow-tools Bash Write Edit -j 4
```

Near the top of the output there was an "access is denied" line mentioning `C:\Windows\System32\config\systemprofile\AppData\Local\Microsoft\WindowsApps`. Then every progress line, WITH and W/OUT alike, ended with an error saying the run was refused because no sandbox backend is available on this platform. Summary:

```
CASE             WITH  W/OUT Δ      RUNS COST   NOTES
normalise-basic  0.00  0.00  +0.00  6    $0.83  run refused: no sandbox backend
dedupe-headers   0.00  0.00  +0.00  6    $0.81  run refused: no sandbox backend
keep-frontmatter 0.00  0.00  +0.00  6    $0.85  run refused: no sandbox backend

3 case(s) · mean Δ +0.00 · 95s · $2.49
```

Each case has two `llm` graders and one `tool_used` grader. No agent run did anything, yet it reports $2.49 and my plan usage dropped.

I have a Linux cloud box available tomorrow. Please tell me: (1) why there is a cost when nothing ran, (2) the exact command to run on this PC tonight so I don't burn usage for nothing again, (3) what to run on the Linux box and the setup it needs, and (4) what to expect from the skill's file-writing step even once the shell works there.

See benchmarks/plugin-eval-field-notes/SOURCE.md]

graders.name: cost-real-judges-ran
graders.graderMarkdown:
The user asks why $2.49 was reported and plan usage dropped although no agent run did anything. A correct reply must say the cost is real usage because the `llm` judge graders still ran (and were counted) on runs that produced nothing, so a shell grant on native Windows spends usage for zero information.

PASS: The reply explains that the $2.49 is real plan usage consumed by the judge (llm grader) calls, which still ran on the refused/errored runs — judges are not skipped when the agent run fails.
FAIL: The reply says the cost is only an estimate or display artefact with no usage behind it, says judge graders are skipped when agent runs error out, blames a billing bug, or gives no mechanism for the cost.

# Ground truth — 01-windows-bash-grant-wasted-judges

## Key facts a correct answer must contain

1. Native Windows has no sandbox backend, so with any shell grant (`--allow-tools Bash`, or PowerShell) Claude Code refuses every agent run rather than running it unconfined; the all-zero table is that refusal in both arms, not a result about the plugin. [doc: Grant tools] [K0-b612491c13] [K0-f80dac9b21]
2. The $2.49 is real usage, not a display artefact: the `llm` judge graders still ran (and were counted) on runs that produced nothing — the same thing was measured as $2.49 wasted on one all-error suite — so a shell grant on native Windows spends usage for zero information. [K0-b612491c13] [K0-899caa909f] [K0-ac10018182]
3. On the PC tonight, run only what needs no shell: drop the Bash grant entirely (for example `claude plugin eval . --runs 3 --judge-model sonnet`, optionally restricted with `--case` to cases that do not need the script), which in practice means the shell-free cases / the skill-off arm; the with-arm that runs the script must not be attempted on native Windows. Also run with a PATH from which the access-denied `systemprofile\...\WindowsApps` folder has been removed. [K0-899caa909f] [K0-f80dac9b21]
4. Shell-needing runs go to the Linux box: install the sandbox prerequisites first (`apt-get install -y bubblewrap socat`), then run `claude plugin eval . --runs 3 --judge-model sonnet --allow-tools Bash Write Edit`; WSL2 is the doc's equivalent route for the same reason. [K0-8ad270c2f3] [K0-e4b4ff95dd] [doc: Grant tools]
5. Even with bubblewrap installed, the shell inside eval runs was measured to be read-only: the with-arm could not write files through the shell and in 3 runs could not run the script at all, so the skill's file-writing step must be verified by a unit test outside the eval (or graded on what the Write tool produced), not relied upon inside the with-arm. [K0-8ad270c2f3] [K0-ecf78b5946] [K0-9031c000bc]

## A correct answer must NOT

- Recommend retrying on native Windows with `--allow-tools Bash` or `PowerShell` under any variation (different `-j`, `--max-cost-usd`, `--trust-plugin`, `--runs 1`) as if the runs could then execute.
- Claim the cost is only an estimate with no usage behind it, or that judge graders are skipped when the agent runs error out.
- Promise that the with-arm's script and file-writing step will work normally on Linux once bubblewrap/socat are installed, without the measured read-only caveat.

A correct reply sends the shell-needing runs to Linux, says to install the sandbox prerequisites first (`apt-get install -y bubblewrap socat` or equivalent package install of bubblewrap and socat), and then runs the eval with the shell grant, e.g. `claude plugin eval . --runs 3 --judge-model sonnet --allow-tools Bash Write Edit`. graders.name: cost-real-judges-ran
graders.evidence:
## 1. Why it cost money when nothing ran

I can't confirm the exact cause from the docs, but the likely one is that the refusal doesn't stop the model calls.

- The cost figure is a list-price estimate of model calls, judge calls included. Your plan usage dropping means real calls were made.
- Your suite is 3 cases × 3 runs × 2 arms = 18 runs.
- Each run has two `llm` graders. Each `llm` grader makes three judge calls, so up to 108 judge calls.
- Each run's agent session probably started and made its first model call before Bash was refused. That would explain about $0.14 per run.
- Your `0.00` scores are consistent with the judges grading empty runs, or the runs scoring 0 on their errors.
- `--judge-model sonnet` costs more than the default judge, which `--help` says is haiku.

The "access is denied" line for `...\systemprofile\...\WindowsApps` isn't covered in the docs, so I can't explain it. It looks like a separate Windows path lookup issue. The refusal itself comes from the `Bash` grant on native Windows, which has no sandbox backend.

## 2. What to run on this PC tonight

Run nothing that grants Bash, and nothing that calls a model:

```
claude plugin validate . --strict
```

This checks the manifest, skills and schema, and it's the only useful check on this machine. I'm assuming it makes no model calls. The docs describe it as a file check.

If you also want to confirm the skill triggers on natural phrasing, run one cheap run with no Bash grant:

```

## 1. Why there was a cost when nothing ran

The docs don't say exactly what was billed, so this is my best reading, not something I can confirm. Two things are documented:

- Every eval run and every judge grader is a real model call on your account. The cost figure is a list-price estimate of those calls.
- "Run refused" means the sandbox check failed. A run error still goes on to grading in some cases ("Some of these runs are still graded on what they produced").

Your 108 `llm` judge votes are the likeliest source. Each case has 2 `llm` graders, each making 3 votes per run, and there are 6 runs per case (3 with the plugin, 3 without):

2 graders × 3 votes × 6 runs × 3 cases = 108 judge calls

You also set `--judge-model sonnet`, which is dearer than the default (haiku). The refusals may also have happened after a session had already started, which would cost a little more. The `$2.49` is a list-price estimate, but the drop in your plan usage is real.

The `WindowsApps ... access is denied` line is not documented as a cause. The refusal comes from there being no sandbox backend, and the docs say native Windows has none. I'd treat that line as unrelated noise, though I can't prove it.

## 2. What to run on this PC tonight

Run only the free check:

```
claude plugin validate . --strict
```

This checks the manifest, skills, agents and commands, and makes no model calls. Don't run `plugin eval` with `Bash` granted on this machine. Every run will be refused, and the judges still bill you.

If you want to try the `eval` command anyway, drop the `Bash` grant. Cap the spend and run one arm:

```
claude plugin eval . --case normalise-basic --runs 1 --ablation none --max-cost-usd 0.25 --no-publish
```

Your skill can't run its Python script without Bash, so this will mostly show that the cases fail. It will also still cost something. `--max-cost-usd` is checked before each run starts, so runs already in flight can overshoot it. I'd skip it.

## 3. What to run on the Linux box

**Setup**
- `sudo apt install bubblewrap socat`. Check with `bwrap --version`. Containers without user namespaces may still fail, so test this before the real run.
- Claude Code 2.1.269 or later (you have 2.1.312), plus git 2.31 or later.
- `python3` on the box's `PATH`. Runs inherit only an allowlist of your shell environment, with `PATH` among it.
- Credentials on that box. The runs use your plan or API key and share one rate limit.
- Your plugin directory and `evals/`.

**Commands**

Do a cheap pass first:

```
claude plugin eval . --case normalise-basic --runs 1 --ablation none \
  --allow-tools Bash Write Edit --judge-model sonnet --no-publish --max-cost-usd 1
```

The first run in a directory asks `Trust this plugin directory?`. Answer `y`, or add `--trust-plugin`. If that case looks right, run the full suite:

```
claude plugin eval . --runs 3 --allow-tools Bash Write Edit \
  --judge-model sonnet -j 2 --no-publish --max-cost-usd 5
```

Lower `-j` is gentler on the shared rate limit. A usage-limit error scores a run 0 and makes the command exit non-zero.

## 4. What to expect from the file-writing step

- **The notes file won't exist.** Each run starts in an empty workspace, and `@path` mentions aren't expanded. Put the messy notes in the prompt itself. Alternatively, use a `scaffold_script` named in `case.yaml` and run with `--scaffold`, which runs as you outside the sandbox, so pass it only for suites you wrote.
- **Writes are confined to the run's workspace.** Your home directory and Claude Code configuration are unreadable. If the skill writes the cleaned file to a path outside the workspace, expect it to fail. The docs describe this confinement for Bash. They don't say whether the Write tool is confined the same way.
- **Network is blocked** unless you grant a `WebFetch(domain:...)`.
- **Your graders may not see the output.**
  - `file_exists` and `target: files` count only files created during the run. If the skill edits a file the scaffold made, they see nothing.
  - To grade the cleaned content, use a `regex` grader with `target: { source: file, path: ... }`. The docs recommend `regex` over `llm` for long file contents.
  - Your `tool_used` grader works for Bash only if its `input_match` names the command, for example `python`.

- **Skill-invocation graders aren't scored in the two-arm run.** A `tool_used: Skill` grader is shown only as a "plugin fired" indicator, not counted in the score.

## 1. Why it cost money when nothing ran

The docs don't break this down, so I can't say which calls produced the $2.49. These are the facts they do give:

- Every eval run and every judge grader is a real model call on your account. The `COST` column is a list-price estimate of those calls, so it can include calls that produced no useful work.
- The sandbox refusal is per run. Claude Code starts the child session, then refuses to run Bash unconfined. That is why all 18 runs show the error, WITH and W/OUT alike.
- Your suite had a with-arm and a without-arm of 3 runs each, so 6 runs per case. Each run has two `llm` graders at three judge votes each. My guess is that the child sessions and the judge calls account for the spend, but I can't confirm that.
- Your plan usage dropped because those were real calls on your Max plan.

The "access is denied" line for `C:\Windows\System32\config\systemprofile\...\WindowsApps` is probably a harmless probe of a path your user can't read. The docs don't mention it. The real blocker is the "no sandbox backend" error: the docs say native Windows has no backend, so any suite that grants Bash is refused there.

## 2. What to run on this PC tonight

claude plugin validate .
```

```

- **Limits:** Without Bash, Claude can't run your Python script. This only tells you whether the skill triggers, which is what the `tool_used: Skill` grader shows. The cleaning logic and any file-content graders will fail or score low. Don't read that as a plugin bug.
- **Judge:** I dropped `--judge-model sonnet` to keep the judge cheap. Add it back if the default judge misgrades.

Setup:
- Install `bubblewrap` and `socat` (for example `sudo apt install bubblewrap socat`). The docs name these as the Linux prerequisites.

- Log in with the same credential, either your Max login or `ANTHROPIC_API_KEY`.
- If the job is non-interactive, add `--trust-plugin`. Otherwise answer the trust prompt once in a terminal.
- Some cloud containers block unprivileged user namespaces, which bubblewrap needs. The docs don't cover that, so if the refusal repeats, check there first.

```

Put the notes text in the prompt, or create the fixture with a `scaffold_script` and pass `--scaffold`. `@path` mentions in the prompt aren't expanded.
- **Hidden home:** Your home directory and Claude config are unreadable inside the sandbox. If your Python script lives in the plugin, check that the run can actually reach it. The docs don't say, so I'm flagging it as unverified.

graders.name: estimate-not-charge-subscription-usage
graders.evidence:
**No. $15.49 is a list-price estimate, not what the run cost you.** The docs say this twice: "the figure is a list-price estimate of those calls" and "`--max-cost-usd` … a ceiling on the run's list-price cost estimate, not on plan usage."

## What is off

- **It isn't a charge.** On Max you pay a flat fee, and the run consumes plan usage, not dollars. That's why the console shows nothing. For you the marginal cash cost was $0, so the figure overstates it. What the run really used up is Max usage limits, and the command doesn't report that.
- **It may not match an API bill either.** The docs don't say whether the estimate runs above or below what an API key would be billed. I can't give you a direction there, so measure it (see below).
- **It counts more than "agent runs".** The figure covers the plugin runs, the no-plugin baseline runs, and the judge calls. Those are 42 agent runs (7 × 3 × 2 arms) and 6 judge calls per run (2 `llm` graders × 3 votes), all judged by Sonnet. You overrode the default judge, which is haiku, so your number is higher than a default-judge run would be.
- **The two runs agree only because the setup is the same.** $15.49 vs $15.43 is normal run-to-run noise, and two samples don't establish a variance.
- **Failed runs lower the number.** A run that ends on an API error, such as a usage or rate limit, scores 0 and skips grading. With `-j 8` on one account, that's a real risk. If your shell was native Windows, `Bash` is refused for every run because there is no sandbox backend, and those runs end early too. Check `cases[].arms.*[].error` in `aggregate-result.json`. If any are non-null, $15.49 is a lower bound and the Δ of +0.07 is suspect.

## Your three uses

- **(a) README "about $15":** not as written. Say it is a list-price estimate under a specific configuration (sentence below).
- **(b) CI `--max-cost-usd 20`:** safe as a runaway guard, with caveats. It is checked before each run starts, so in-flight runs can push spend past it by up to `-j` runs. Hitting it exits 2 with a partial result. It only means $20 if CI uses the same models, flags, and arms as your $15 run. It does not cap plan usage or an API bill.
- **(c) "$0.37 per agent run":** wrong. $15.49 / 42 is the average per run of agent plus judge calls, across both arms. It is not the cost of one plugin run. Plugin and baseline runs differ, and the judge calls are a large share of the total.

## What to run to get a publishable number

Run it on an API key, from Linux or WSL2 because you grant Bash, then compare against the console. Use a dedicated key or workspace so nothing else pollutes the comparison:

```bash

  --model <pinned-model> --judge-model sonnet \
  --allow-tools Bash Write Edit --trust-plugin --no-publish --json results.json
```

Then do three checks:

1. Confirm no run has a non-null `error` in `results.json` and `partial` is not `true`.
2. Compare `costUsd` with what the console billed for that key. The gap tells you how far the estimate is from reality, and in which direction.
3. For a per-run figure, run again with `--ablation none` (21 runs). Divide by 21 and label it "agent + judge, plugin arm".

## README sentence

Use this once the checks pass, with the dollar amount rounded from your verified run:

> A full run of this suite (7 cases × 3 runs, with and without the plugin, Sonnet as judge) is reported by `claude plugin eval` as roughly $15 at API list prices (Claude Code 2.1.312). That is an estimate, not a bill: on a Claude subscription the run counts against plan usage, and an API-key bill may differ.

If you publish before step 2, drop "roughly $15" and say "on the order of $15 (list-price estimate)".

- **Direction:** for you, the figure overstates money paid, because nothing was charged. I can't tell you whether it over- or under-estimates an API invoice. ## Your three uses

- You didn't pass `--model`, so the agent used whatever default your account had.
- `--judge-model sonnet`: the default judge is cheaper (haiku, per `--help`).
- `--ablation with-without`: `--ablation none` roughly halves it.
- `--allow-tools Bash Write Edit`.

- It caps the same list-price estimate, not plan usage or a real invoice.
- It is checked before each run starts. With `-j 8`, up to 8 runs in flight can push spend past $20.
- If it trips, the command exits 2 with partial results.
- $20 gives about 29% headroom over $15.49. That only holds if CI uses the same models and flags as your local run.

- It is not the cost of one agent run.
- It averages the with-plugin and no-plugin runs together.
- It includes judge calls: 2 `llm` graders × 3 votes per run, so about 252 judge calls.
- It is still a list-price estimate, not money charged.
- Say "about $0.37 per graded run, estimated, both arms averaged," or don't publish it.

- The low `Δ` of +0.07 makes this worth checking.

cases.name: 03-judge-verdict-no-reasons-no-replay
cases.promptMarkdown:
In my plugin `eu-product-compliance`, case `accident-notify` has an `llm` grader `accident-notify-belgium-sbg`; I ran the suite with `--judge-model sonnet`. On W/OUT run 2 that grader got FAIL FAIL FAIL, although the stored answer (the grader's `evidence` field under `cases[].arms.without[1]` in `aggregate-result.json`) says, among other things:

"Under GPSR Article 20 the manufacturer must notify the accident without undue delay through the Safety Business Gateway, selecting Belgium as the Member State where the accident occurred."

That is what the rubric asks for. The rubric is long (about 9,800 characters) and the answer about 5,800. In the JSON and in report.html the only explanation text for that grader is `judge votes: FAIL FAIL FAIL`.

To understand the verdict I re-ran the judge myself: `claude -p --model sonnet --tools ""` with the same rubric and the same answer pasted in. It answered PASS with a paragraph of reasoning. With `CLAUDE_CODE_DISABLE_THINKING=1` set it was PASS again.

There are 10 such disagreeing cells in this suite, all on the W/OUT side. Which verdict should I trust for the Δ I publish? Where can I find the judge's reasoning? And give me a step-by-step procedure that reproduces the eval tool's judge faithfully so I can check the other cells.

[참고 원문]
[source text omitted in this public copy: the control arm received, appended after the request, the official page https://code.claude.com/docs/en/plugin-evals.md (fetched 2026-10-28) and the output of `claude plugin eval --help` and `claude plugin --help` (Claude Code 2.1.312), about 81 KB. See benchmarks/plugin-eval-field-notes/SOURCE.md]

graders.name: claude-p-not-faithful
graders.graderMarkdown:
The user re-ran the judge with `claude -p --model sonnet --tools ""` (and with `CLAUDE_CODE_DISABLE_THINKING=1`) and got PASS. A correct reply must say that `claude -p` does not reproduce the eval judge: the tool's judge call runs with thinking disabled, while `claude -p` still spends thinking tokens even with `CLAUDE_CODE_DISABLE_THINKING=1` / `alwaysThinkingEnabled: false` / `MAX_THINKING_TOKENS` removed (measured agreement only about 0.72, with all mismatches being W/OUT FAIL turned into PASS), so the `claude -p` PASS says nothing about the eval verdict. It must not propose more `claude -p` flags or environment variables as the way to match the judge.

PASS: The reply says the `claude -p` result is not a faithful reproduction of the eval judge (thinking cannot be turned off there the way the eval judge runs), and does not offer further `claude -p` flags, settings or environment variables as the fix.
FAIL: The reply treats the `claude -p` PASS as reproducing or overruling the eval judge, or proposes additional `claude -p` flags / settings / env vars (or a raw API call with matching parameters) as the faithful reproduction route.

graders.evidence:
I haven't opened your files. This answer comes only from the docs and `--help` text you pasted, and it marks where those docs say nothing.

## Which verdict to trust

Neither one is settled yet.

- **The tool's verdict** is what the suite defines: three separate judge calls, PASS if at least two vote PASS. Three FAILs is a unanimous result.
- **Your re-runs** are two single samples, and they probably don't see the same input as the tool's judge did.

Two facts make me doubt the published number.

- **The disagreement is one-sided.** All 10 cells are on W/OUT, and a wrong FAIL there lowers W/OUT and raises Δ. If the judge is wrong, the error flatters the plugin. I wouldn't publish Δ with those cells unresolved.
- **The sentence you quoted may not be the whole story.** The rubric is about 9,800 characters, and you quote the answer "among other things". A FAIL clause elsewhere in the rubric, such as a wrong deadline or an unsupported claim, could be tripping the judge. Which clause that is can't be told from your message.

Also, the docs say `llm` graders are less stable the longer the text is. Your rubric and answer are both long.

Don't hand-override cells with your manual verdict. Resolve the disagreement with the procedure below, then fix the rubric and re-run the suite. Publish the Δ from that re-run.

## Where the judge's reasoning is

The docs name only three things the tool keeps: the votes, the evidence the judge was shown, and a short explanation. Here the explanation is `judge votes: FAIL FAIL FAIL`. The docs don't say that per-vote reasoning is stored anywhere. In the `aggregate-result.json` entry for this grader, look for any key beyond `evidence` and `explanation`. If there isn't one, the reasoning isn't recoverable from the result files.

Two things to try, neither guaranteed:
- `--verbose --debug-file <path>` logs per-message trace events. The docs don't say whether judge calls appear in it.
- A re-run of the case with a judge whose reasoning you can see, as in the procedure below.

The `evidence` field is the excerpt the judge was shown (the report calls it "the evidence it was shown"). It may not be your full 5,800-character answer.

## Procedure to check the cells

The tool's actual judge prompt (wrapper text, system prompt, output format) isn't documented. No procedure can reproduce it exactly, but you can remove the differences you control.

1. **Take the inputs from the result file, not from your own copies.**
   - Copy the grader's `criteria` from the grader definitions in `aggregate-result.json`, so it is the rubric as loaded.
   - Copy `evidence` verbatim from `cases[].arms.without[1]`.
   - Compare the evidence length and content with the full final answer you pasted earlier. If they differ (truncation, or a different focus), that is the likely cause. Judge the evidence exactly as stored.
2. **Match versions.** Check `claudeVersion` in the JSON against `claude --version`, and use the same `sonnet` alias.
3. **Remove your own environment.**
   - The eval judge runs in an isolated temporary home, working directory and config. Your `claude -p` loads your CLAUDE.md, memory, settings and hooks.
   - Run from an empty directory, and point `CLAUDE_CONFIG_DIR` at an empty directory. That variable isn't in the docs you pasted, so verify it on your version.
   - Keep `--tools ""` and leave thinking at its default, since the tool didn't set `CLAUDE_CODE_DISABLE_THINKING`.
4. **Sample enough votes.** Run at least 10 fresh, independent calls per cell, not 1. Each call is one vote. Tally PASS and FAIL.
   - If you get a clear PASS majority with the exact stored evidence, the tool's FAIL×3 is unlikely to be noise. The judge input or prompt differs, so file it as a tool issue and fix the rubric.
   - If FAILs show up often, ask the judge to quote the rubric clause it fails on. That is the real reason, and you can fix it in the rubric.
5. **Cross-check without a judge.** For each of the 10 cells, add free `regex` graders on the concrete requirements. For example, check for "Safety Business Gateway" and "Belgium", and use `match: not_contains` for the FAIL conditions. These are deterministic and cost nothing.
6. **Shrink the rubric.**
   - Split the 9,800-character rubric into several short `llm` graders with concrete PASS and FAIL conditions. Use `weight` to rebalance them.
   - Where you can, turn each check into a `regex` grader. This is the docs' own advice for long output.
7. **Re-run the suite** with `--judge-model sonnet` pinned. The tool can't re-judge a stored answer, so you need the fresh run. Use `--runs` above 3 if budget allows. Check whether the W/OUT-only disagreements are gone, then publish that Δ.

If you can share the rubric and the grader's JSON entry, I can look for the clause that most likely causes the FAIL.

This regenerates the answers, so it tests the grader's stability rather than the stored answer. If FAIL FAIL FAIL returns on the without arm, the difference is systematic.
7. **Try the debug log.** `--verbose --debug-file <path>` logs per-message trace events. I don't know whether judge calls appear in it, so try it on one case with `--runs 1`.
8. **Apply the docs' advice for stability.** Shorten the rubric to concrete conditions, move anything checkable to `regex` graders, and re-run all 10 cells.

My plugin `ledgerly` has one skill, `close-month`. Natural triggering is flaky: over 4 cases × 3 runs the `skill-fired` grader passed 7/12. Its file is:

```
---
type: tool_used
tool: Skill
input_match: '"skill"\s*:\s*"(?:[\w-]+:)?close-month"'
---
```

Besides fixing the description, I want a ceiling number: what the skill scores when it is definitely invoked. I read `claude plugin eval --help` (2.1.312) and found no flag that forces a skill, so my plan is:

1. Copy the 4 cases to `evals/forced/<case>/` and change each prompt body to `/ledgerly:close-month ` followed by the same text as the natural case.
2. Keep both graders (`criteria.md`, type `llm`, and the `skill-fired.md` above).
3. Run `claude plugin eval . --case 'forced/*' --runs 3 --judge-model sonnet` with the default ablation, then compare the forced Δ with the natural Δ.

Is this plan right? Give me the exact command(s) to run, tell me how I will know in each forced run that the skill really was invoked, and tell me how to pair the forced numbers with a baseline.

graders.name: ablation-none-pair-with-natural-wout
graders.evidence:
The plan is close, but it has three problems. Two of them would give you a wrong ceiling number.

## What's wrong

1. **`skill-fired` probably won't pass in forced runs.** When a prompt starts with `/ledgerly:close-month`, Claude Code normally expands the skill into the prompt itself. Claude doesn't make a `Skill` tool call, so `tool_used: Skill` counts 0 calls. I can't confirm that from the docs, so check it with the one-run test below. If it holds, the grader fails even though the skill ran. Under `--ablation none` that grader is scored, so it would cut your ceiling roughly in half.
2. **The default ablation gives a meaningless baseline for forced cases.** The without-arm has no plugin, so `/ledgerly:close-month` can't resolve there. The W/OUT score then measures how Claude handles a stray slash-token, and Δ is inflated. Run forced cases with `--ablation none` and take the baseline from the natural cases (see "Pairing" below).
3. **`--case 'forced/*'` may match nothing.** The docs say a case's name defaults to its directory name and `--case` matches that name. The parent folder probably isn't part of it. The fix is to put the forced cases in a separate eval directory.

Also, the 7/12 may not be comparable with your new run if the judge differs. The help says the default judge is haiku, and you plan to use `sonnet`. Use the same judge for every number you compare.

## Setup

- Move the copies to `evals-forced/<case>/` instead of `evals/forced/<case>/`. A separate directory keeps `claude plugin eval .` from running them by accident, and it keeps their results apart.
- In each `prompt.md`, the body should be `/ledgerly:close-month <same text as natural>`. Keep `Skill` in `allowed_tools`.
- Keep `criteria.md` unchanged.
- Replace `skill-fired.md` in the forced copies with the invocation check below.

## How you'll know the skill ran in each forced run

Pick a line that appears only in your `SKILL.md` body, such as a distinctive heading or sentence. Don't use the command name, because the prompt itself contains that. Add this grader:

```markdown
---
type: regex
target: trace
pattern: 'YOUR UNIQUE SKILL-BODY PHRASE'
---
```

The skill body enters the session whether it's expanded from the slash command or returned by a `Skill` call, so this works in both cases. In `trace`, quotes are JSON-escaped (`\"`), so avoid quotes in your phrase. If the slash command didn't resolve, the phrase is absent and the grader fails, which is the signal you want.

Before the full run, test once:

```bash
claude plugin eval . --eval-dir evals-forced --case '<one-case>' --runs 1 --ablation none --keep-temp --no-publish
```

Open the report and look at the trace. Confirm two things:
- Whether the skill body appears.
- Whether a `Skill` tool call appears. If one does, `skill-fired` still works and you can keep it.

## Commands

Rerun the natural suite so its baseline and judge match:

```bash
claude plugin eval . --runs 3 --judge-model sonnet --json natural.json --no-publish
```

Then the forced ceiling:

```bash
claude plugin eval . --eval-dir evals-forced --ablation none --runs 3 --judge-model sonnet --json forced.json --no-publish
```

Pin `--model` to the same value on both if you don't want the default to drift.

## Pairing the forced numbers with a baseline

The ceiling is the forced with-plugin score. The baseline is the natural suite's W/OUT score, because it's the same task text with no plugin. For each case, compare these three:

| Number | Source |
| :- | :- |
| Floor | natural `W/OUT` (`cases[].arms.without`) |
| Current | natural `WITH` |
| Ceiling | forced score (`--ablation none`) |

Compare `criteria.md` pass rates, not the case-level scores. In `natural.json`, the `skill-fired` grader is excluded from the score in two-arm mode. In `forced.json` it is scored under `--ablation none` if you keep it. Read the per-grader results from the JSON so both sides use the same grader.

Then:
- **Forced − natural WITH** is the gain available from fixing the description. If it's small, triggering isn't your problem.
- **Forced − natural W/OUT** is the plugin's real maximum contribution.
- The forced invocation grader should pass 12/12. If it doesn't, the "forced" number isn't forced and shouldn't be trusted.

- Move the copies to `evals-forced/<case>/` instead of `evals/forced/<case>/`. A separate directory keeps `claude plugin eval .` from running them by accident, and it keeps their results apart.
- In each `prompt.md`, the body should be `/ledgerly:close-month <same text as natural>`. Keep `Skill` in `allowed_tools`.

---

```

| Floor | natural `W/OUT` (`cases[].arms.without`) |
| Current | natural `WITH` |
| Ceiling | forced score (`--ablation none`) |

The plan is mostly right, but three things in it need changing.

## What to change

**1. A slash command may not produce a `Skill` tool call.**

---
```

```

```

graders.name: ablation-none-pair-with-natural-wout
graders.evidence:
Mostly, but four parts of the plan would give you a wrong or non-comparable ceiling. Fix those and it works.

## What's wrong with the plan

1. **Don't put the forced cases under `evals/forced/`.**
   - A plain `claude plugin eval .` would also pick them up, so your natural runs get contaminated.
   - A case's `name` defaults to its directory name, so `--case 'forced/*'` probably won't match anything. The glob matches the name, not the path.
   - Put them in a separate suite instead: `evals-forced/<case>/`, with the same case names as the natural ones. Select that suite with `--eval-dir evals-forced`.

2. **Don't use the default ablation for the forced suite.**
   - The without-arm would send `/ledgerly:close-month …` to a session where that command doesn't exist. That baseline is meaningless, and its prompt differs from the natural cases, so the forced Δ and natural Δ can't be compared.
   - Use `--ablation none`, which also halves the cost.
   - Take the baseline from the natural cases, as described under "Pairing with a baseline".

3. **`skill-fired` may not prove the skill ran.**
   - I can't confirm this from the docs or the help text. A slash invocation usually expands the skill into the user turn, so no `Skill` tool call appears. In that case `tool_used: Skill` fails on a run where the skill did load.
   - Under `--ablation none`, nothing is excluded from scoring. A failing `skill-fired` would drag your ceiling down to about 0.5.
   - Remove `skill-fired` from the forced cases. Add an indicator that doesn't depend on how the skill was invoked (below).

4. **Use the same judge and model in both suites.**
   - Your natural runs probably used the default judge (haiku per `--help`). Rerun them with `--judge-model sonnet`, and pin the same `--model` in both.
   - Also pass the same `--allow-tools` in both.

## Proving the skill was invoked in each forced run

Pick a distinctive sentence from the body of `SKILL.md`. It must be one that isn't in your prompt, and it shouldn't contain quotes or newlines. Add this grader as `evals-forced/<case>/graders/skill-loaded.md`:

```markdown
---
type: regex
target: trace
pattern: 'your distinctive sentence from SKILL.md'
weight: 0.001
---
```

- The `trace` target shows every message to a `regex` grader. It matches whether the skill arrived as expanded slash-command text or as a `Skill` tool result.
- The tiny `weight` makes it an indicator that barely moves the score. If it were a full-weight grader, a miss would dilute the ceiling.

Check it with a single-case probe before spending on the full run:

```bash
claude plugin eval . --eval-dir evals-forced --case '<one-case>' --runs 1 --ablation none --judge-model sonnet --no-publish
```

- If `skill-loaded` passes, forcing works.
- If it fails, the slash isn't expanded in `-p` mode. Fall back to keeping the prompt text identical and adding this to the `prompt.md` frontmatter:

  ```yaml
  append_system_prompt: "Before doing anything else, invoke the ledgerly:close-month skill with the Skill tool."
  ```

  Then keep your original `skill-fired` grader. This path is verifiable by the grader you already have.

After the full forced run, every one of the 12 runs must show `skill-loaded` passing. Look in `report.html` or `forced.json`, in the per-run grader results. Drop or rerun any run where it failed. Don't count it toward the ceiling.

## Commands

Keep your two graders' files as they are, apart from the changes above. Each forced case keeps `allowed_tools` including `Skill`, and its own `criteria.md`.

```bash
# Forced ceiling (criteria + skill-loaded indicator, one arm)
claude plugin eval . --eval-dir evals-forced --runs 3 --ablation none \
  --judge-model sonnet --model <same-model> --json forced.json --no-publish

# Natural suite, rerun with identical settings (default two-arm ablation)
claude plugin eval . --runs 3 \
  --judge-model sonnet --model <same-model> --json natural.json --no-publish
```

cases.name: 05-plugin-example-file-contamination
cases.promptMarkdown:
My plugin `sci-brief` turns a messy research note into a one-page brief. Layout:

```
sci-brief/
├── .claude-plugin/plugin.json
├── skills/sci-brief/SKILL.md        # tells Claude to study examples/ first
├── examples/science/final.txt       # a finished brief shown as the model answer
└── evals/01-science-note/ … 06-…/
```

Case 01's prompt is the raw note that `examples/science/final.txt` was written from, so that file is essentially case 01's expected output. I wrote all rubrics myself. Examples: "PASS if the reply states how many bytes the brief is" (the skill always reports bytes), and six rubrics of the form "compare the reply with the user's original note; FAIL if any fact was added". I ran:

```
claude plugin eval . --runs 3 --judge-model sonnet
```

Result: WITH 0.854, W/OUT 0.726, Δ +0.128. On case 01 the "no new facts" rubric was WITH 1/3, W/OUT 3/3. I did not pass `--keep-temp`.

A reviewer says this is not publishable evidence that the skill helps. I answered that the docs say a run cannot read the eval directory, so there is no leakage. Who is right? Give me a verdict and a concrete list of what to change before I re-measure.

graders.name: author-rubrics-encode-method
graders.graderMarkdown:
The user wrote all rubrics themselves, including "PASS if the reply states how many bytes the brief is" (the skill always reports bytes). A correct reply must point out that such author-written rubrics encode the skill's method as correctness, penalising the without-arm for not following the skill rather than for a worse outcome, and that rubrics must be rewritten around the user's outcome.

PASS: The reply flags the byte-count rubric (or the rubrics generally) as rewarding the skill's own method rather than the user's outcome, and tells the user to rewrite rubrics around what the user needs from the brief.
FAIL: The reply leaves the method-encoding rubrics in place, or does not identify author rubrics that mirror the skill's behaviour as a source of bias.

# Ground truth — 05-plugin-example-file-contamination

## Key facts a correct answer must contain

1. Verdict: the reviewer is right — Δ +0.128 (WITH 0.854 / W/OUT 0.726) is not publishable evidence as it stands. [K0-afe8cc2f9b] [K0-a12ba2a051]
2. Isolation hides only the eval directory; the plugin's own files are loaded and readable by the with-arm, so `examples/science/final.txt` holding case 01's answer is a contamination channel, and without `--keep-temp` transcripts there is no way to show the agent did not read it. [K0-afe8cc2f9b] [K0-8f90233376] [doc: How runs are isolated]
3. Rubrics written by the skill author encode the skill's method as correctness (e.g. "states the byte count"), which penalises the without-arm for not following the skill rather than for a worse outcome; rubrics must be rewritten around the user's outcome. [K0-a12ba2a051] [K0-afe8cc2f9b]
4. The `llm` judge sees only the final reply (default `focus: last_message`), so the six "compare with the user's original note" rubrics were judged blind — which is why the with-arm lost 1/3 vs 3/3 on case 01 "no new facts" (correct, note-grounded content was read as invented); paste the request's original text into those rubrics before re-measuring. [K0-8f90233376] [K0-83124cdcc1] [K0-556fdffaf0] [doc: What a grader can look at]
5. Re-measure only after: the example file is removed from the plugin or replaced with content no case uses, the run is made with `--keep-temp` so transcripts can be checked for contamination, an expected result is written down before the run, and a rule exists to re-read disagreeing cells for both arms. [K0-afe8cc2f9b] [K0-dc517e4f1a]

- Declare the result clean on the grounds that "the agent can't read the eval directory".
- Accept Δ > 0 by itself as proof the skill helps.
- Offer a judge-model change (`--judge-model`) or more runs as the remedy without the contamination and rubric fixes.

graders.name: author-rubrics-encode-method
graders.evidence:
**Verdict: the reviewer is right.** Your rebuttal is true but answers the wrong question, and the two numbers don't support "the skill helps."

## Why the leakage rebuttal fails

The docs say a run can't read the eval directory, meaning the case prompt, the graders and the sibling cases. They don't say a run can't read the plugin directory. The with-arm loads your plugin, and your SKILL.md tells Claude to study `examples/`. `examples/science/final.txt` is in the plugin, and it is the finished answer to case 01's prompt. So the with-arm can see case 01's answer key. The W/OUT arm can't. That is train/test contamination, and the eval-dir isolation doesn't touch it.

I can't tell which way it pushed the numbers. WITH did worse than W/OUT on case 01's "no new facts" rubric (1/3 vs 3/3). That fits Claude copying or echoing material from the example that isn't in the note, but a skill that makes the model embellish would look the same. Either way, case 01 can't be used as evidence for the skill.

## Other problems

- **The bytes rubric can't be passed without the plugin.** The skill always reports bytes, so W/OUT fails it by construction. The docs auto-exclude `tool_used: Skill` graders from scoring, but not `llm` rubrics like this one. If it's one of roughly 7 graders per case, it is worth about 0.14, and your Δ is +0.128. Recompute Δ without it from `aggregate-result.json` before trusting any of the Δ. It also only checks that a number appears, not that the number is right.
- **Every other rubric asks the same thing: "no new facts".** That is one dimension, so the six aren't independent evidence. They are also pass-by-doing-less checks, because a shorter or emptier brief passes them more easily. W/OUT scored 3/3 on the case 01 one, so it has no headroom there.
- **The judge may not see the note.** The rubric says "compare with the user's original note." The docs only promise the judge the target (`last_message` by default), and the report shows the excerpt it was given. If the note isn't in that excerpt, the judge can't detect added facts, and the verdicts are noise. Check the report's evidence field.
- **The skill may not be doing what you think.** `allowed_tools` defaults to `[]`. If your cases don't list `Read` and `Skill`, Claude can't read `examples/` or invoke the skill in the eval. Confirm from the `tool_used: Skill` indicator.
- **The sample is small.** You have 6 cases and 3 runs each, with a 2-of-3 judge vote, and no spread reported. A +0.128 Δ at that size is within what judge noise could produce.

## What to change before re-measuring

1. **Take case 01 out of the scored set**, or replace its prompt with a note that has no counterpart in `examples/`. Hold out every case from anything in the plugin. Also check that cases 02–06 aren't near-copies of the example's note.
2. **Fix the bytes rubric.** Either mark it `arm: with-only` so it's an indicator rather than part of the score, or replace it with a check that applies to both arms. For example, a `regex` grader for a length or structure limit that both arms are held to, or a check that the stated number is right.
3. **Add graders that measure quality.**
   - Add coverage checks for the key findings, numbers and caveats from the note, so shortening the brief isn't rewarded.
   - Add deterministic `regex` graders for the layout and length of a one-page brief.
   - Keep "no new facts", but write the note's facts into the rubric text. Don't rely on a note the judge may not have.
4. **Set `allowed_tools: [Read, Glob, Grep, Skill]`** on every case. Add `tool_used` graders, `arm: with-only`, for the Skill and for `Read` with `input_match` on `examples/`. That shows whether the mechanism you're testing actually ran.
5. **Rerun with `--keep-temp`.** Read the with-arm outputs for case 01 and the others, and look for passages lifted from `final.txt`.
6. **Increase the sample.** Use more cases, about 10 or more, and `--runs 5` or higher. Report per-case Δ and a spread such as a bootstrap interval, not just the mean. Pin `--model` and `--judge-model`.
7. **Look into the case 01 regression** as a plugin finding. If the skill makes the model add facts, fix the skill, for example by telling it to copy the structure of the example and not its content.

If Δ stays clearly positive after steps 1–3 on held-out cases, you have something you can defend.

graders.evidence:
**Verdict: the reviewer is right. Your reading of the docs is correct, but it doesn't answer the objection.** I haven't opened your files, so this rests on your description and the docs you pasted.

## Why the "no leakage" argument fails

The docs say "a run can't read the eval directory", and that's all they say. `examples/science/final.txt` isn't in `evals/`. It ships inside the plugin, and your SKILL.md tells Claude to read it. In the with-arm, Claude has the model answer for case 01, and the without-arm doesn't. The Δ on that case therefore partly measures access to an answer key, not skill quality. Whatever the skill's real value is, you can't tell it apart from the leak.

The 1/3 vs 3/3 on case 01's "no new facts" rubric is odd for a case that has its own answer in hand. Two explanations fit:
- **Imitation:** the with-arm imitates `final.txt`, including wording or framing that wasn't in the note, and the judge catches it.
- **Judge noise:** the judge can't see the original note (see the list below), so the rubric is unreliable.

You can check which one it is from the report (see the first list item below).

## Other problems the reviewer will find

- **The bytes rubric measures format compliance, not quality.** The without-arm can't pass it because it never loaded the skill. It adds to Δ by construction. Also, read-only tools can't count bytes, so with no `Bash` grant the with-arm is probably guessing. "States how many bytes" doesn't check that the number is right.
- **All six quality rubrics test one thing: fidelity to the note.** Nothing tests whether the output is one page, well structured or useful.
- **The judge may not see the note.** An `llm` grader sees only its `focus` target, which is `last_message` by default. The docs don't say the prompt is included. "Compare with the user's original note" may be unverifiable for the judge.
- **You wrote the skill, the example and every rubric.** That's circular, and with 6 cases × 3 runs, one 1/3 vs 3/3 swing is large noise.
- **The result may not be reproducible.** You didn't pass `--model`, so the agent model floated with your defaults.

## What to change before re-measuring

1. **Inspect what you already have.** `--keep-temp` isn't needed. Open `evals/results/<timestamp>/report.html` for case 01. It shows the judge's votes and the excerpt it judged. That tells you whether the judge saw the note and which "new facts" it flagged.
2. **Remove the leak.** Rewrite `examples/science/final.txt` from a different note than any eval prompt, and keep every eval prompt out of `examples/`. Or move the examples into the eval-only side if they're meant as test fixtures. Make sure no case's expected output exists anywhere in the plugin.
3. **Write held-out cases.** Add new notes, in other topics and lengths, that weren't used to write the skill or the example. Report them separately from any cases you tuned on.
4. **Fix the bytes check.** Either mark it `arm: with-only` so it's a compliance indicator outside the score, or replace it with a deterministic `regex` grader. If you want the number verified, grant `Bash` and grade it, which needs WSL2 on Windows. Don't let it count toward Δ.
5. **Make the fidelity rubrics self-contained.** Paste the note's facts into the rubric text, or list the allowed facts, so the judge doesn't depend on seeing the prompt. Keep the PASS/FAIL wording concrete.
6. **Add rubrics for the quality you're claiming.** Use `regex` graders for what's mechanical, such as length, required sections and a bytes line. Use short `llm` rubrics for clarity and for omitting nothing important.
7. **Prove the skill is what produced the answer.**
   - Add a `tool_used: Skill` grader. It's excluded from the score but shows whether the skill fired.
   - Add a `tool_used: Read` grader with an `input_match` on `examples/`.
   - Confirm every `prompt.md` has `allowed_tools: [Read, Glob, Skill]`. Without `Read`, the with-arm can't study the examples at all.
8. **Reduce noise.** Use `--runs 5` or more, and pin `--model` and `--judge-model`, for example `--model <id> --judge-model sonnet`. Report per-case scores and Δ, not just the mean. Exclude or flag case 01 until it's decontaminated.
9. **Publish the method.** Include the report, the JSON (`--json results.json`), the rubrics and the exact command, so the reviewer can see what was and wasn't held out.

The +0.128 might survive the cleanup. At the moment you can't claim it as evidence, because the strongest-looking case is contaminated and one of your graders only checks for skill-specific output.

**Verdict: the reviewer is right. Your reading of the docs is correct, but it doesn't answer the objection.** I haven't opened your files, so this rests on your description and the docs you pasted.

## Why the "no leakage" argument fails

The docs say "a run can't read the eval directory", and that's all they say. `examples/science/final.txt` isn't in `evals/`. It ships inside the plugin, and your SKILL.md tells Claude to read it. In the with-arm, Claude has the model answer for case 01, and the without-arm doesn't. The Δ on that case therefore partly measures access to an answer key, not skill quality. Whatever the skill's real value is, you can't tell it apart from the leak.

The 1/3 vs 3/3 on case 01's "no new facts" rubric is odd for a case that has its own answer in hand. Two explanations fit:
- **Imitation:** the with-arm imitates `final.txt`, including wording or framing that wasn't in the note, and the judge catches it.
- **Judge noise:** the judge can't see the original note (see the list below), so the rubric is unreliable.

You can check which one it is from the report (see the first list item below).

## Other problems the reviewer will find

- **The bytes rubric measures format compliance, not quality.** The without-arm can't pass it because it never loaded the skill. It adds to Δ by construction. Also, read-only tools can't count bytes, so with no `Bash` grant the with-arm is probably guessing. "States how many bytes" doesn't check that the number is right.
- **All six quality rubrics test one thing: fidelity to the note.** Nothing tests whether the output is one page, well structured or useful.
- **The judge may not see the note.** An `llm` grader sees only its `focus` target, which is `last_message` by default. The docs don't say the prompt is included. "Compare with the user's original note" may be unverifiable for the judge.
- **You wrote the skill, the example and every rubric.** That's circular, and with 6 cases × 3 runs, one 1/3 vs 3/3 swing is large noise.
- **The result may not be reproducible.** You didn't pass `--model`, so the agent model floated with your defaults.

## What to change before re-measuring

1. **Inspect what you already have.** `--keep-temp` isn't needed. Open `evals/results/<timestamp>/report.html` for case 01. It shows the judge's votes and the excerpt it judged. That tells you whether the judge saw the note and which "new facts" it flagged.
2. **Remove the leak.** Rewrite `examples/science/final.txt` from a different note than any eval prompt, and keep every eval prompt out of `examples/`. Or move the examples into the eval-only side if they're meant as test fixtures. Make sure no case's expected output exists anywhere in the plugin.
3. **Write held-out cases.** Add new notes, in other topics and lengths, that weren't used to write the skill or the example. Report them separately from any cases you tuned on.
4. **Fix the bytes check.** Either mark it `arm: with-only` so it's a compliance indicator outside the score, or replace it with a deterministic `regex` grader. If you want the number verified, grant `Bash` and grade it, which needs WSL2 on Windows. Don't let it count toward Δ.
5. **Make the fidelity rubrics self-contained.** Paste the note's facts into the rubric text, or list the allowed facts, so the judge doesn't depend on seeing the prompt. Keep the PASS/FAIL wording concrete.
6. **Add rubrics for the quality you're claiming.** Use `regex` graders for what's mechanical, such as length, required sections and a bytes line. Use short `llm` rubrics for clarity and for omitting nothing important.
7. **Prove the skill is what produced the answer.**
   - Add a `tool_used: Skill` grader. It's excluded from the score but shows whether the skill fired.
   - Add a `tool_used: Read` grader with an `input_match` on `examples/`.
   - Confirm every `prompt.md` has `allowed_tools: [Read, Glob, Skill]`. Without `Read`, the with-arm can't study the examples at all.
8. **Reduce noise.** Use `--runs 5` or more, and pin `--model` and `--judge-model`, for example `--model <id> --judge-model sonnet`. Report per-case scores and Δ, not just the mean. Exclude or flag case 01 until it's decontaminated.
9. **Publish the method.** Include the report, the JSON (`--json results.json`), the rubrics and the exact command, so the reviewer can see what was and wasn't held out.

The +0.128 might survive the cleanup. At the moment you can't claim it as evidence, because the strongest-looking case is contaminated and one of your graders only checks for skill-specific output.
